# Chicken (& Sausage) Jambalaya 🇺🇸

::: {.dish-meta}
**Region:** Louisiana, USA  ·  **Family:** One-pot pilaf (Creole/Cajun)
**Serves:** 6  ·  **Active time:** 45 minutes  ·  **Total:** 1 hour 10 min
:::

Jambalaya is Louisiana in a pot: French, Spanish, West African, and Native
foodways simmered together over a couple of centuries into something entirely its
own. Smoky sausage, chicken, the "holy trinity" of vegetables, and rice cooked in
one pan until every grain is stained with flavor.

## The story

Jambalaya is widely understood as Louisiana's answer to Spanish **paella** —
adapted by cooks who lacked saffron and improvised with local ingredients and
West African rice know-how. Two great schools exist:

- **Creole ("red") jambalaya**, from New Orleans, includes tomatoes — a mark of
  the city's Spanish and Caribbean connections.
- **Cajun ("brown") jambalaya**, from the rural bayou country, skips tomatoes and
  gets its color and depth from meat browned hard in the pot.

This recipe leans Cajun-brown but tells you exactly where to add tomato if you
want to fly the Creole flag.

## Ingredients

- 500 g (1 lb) boneless chicken thighs, in bite-size pieces
- 350 g (¾ lb) **certified gluten-free** andouille or other smoked sausage, sliced
- 2 tbsp oil
- **The trinity:** 1 large onion, 2 celery ribs, 1 green bell pepper — all diced
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tsp Cajun/Creole seasoning, plus 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1 tsp dried thyme, 2 bay leaves, ½ tsp cayenne (to taste)
- 350 g (1.75 cups) long-grain rice
- 750 ml (3 cups) chicken stock
- *(Creole option:* 400 g canned diced tomatoes — reduce stock by ½ cup*)*
- Scallions and parsley, hot sauce, to finish

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Gluten-free · dairy-free:** naturally dairy-free, and the rice cooks in stock
(no roux, unlike gumbo). For gluten-free, use a **certified GF sausage** and a **GF
Cajun/Creole seasoning** — the two most common places wheat sneaks in — and a
gluten-free hot sauce.
:::

## Method

1. Season the chicken with a little of the Cajun seasoning. In a heavy pot or
   Dutch oven, brown the sausage in the oil until its fat renders and the edges
   crisp; remove.
2. Brown the chicken hard in the sausage fat, letting a **deep fond** build on the
   bottom of the pot — in brown jambalaya, this dark crust *is* the color and
   flavor. Remove.
3. Add the trinity and cook 6–8 minutes until soft, scraping up the fond as the
   vegetables release moisture. Add the garlic and all the spices; cook 1 minute.
   *(For Creole, stir in the tomatoes now and cook down 5 minutes.)*
4. Stir in the rice and toast 2 minutes.
5. Return the sausage and chicken with any juices. Pour in the stock, add the bay
   leaves, and stir once to combine and level the rice.
6. Bring to a boil, then cover and drop to the **lowest heat for 25 minutes**.
   Resist stirring — like most pilafs, stirring makes it gummy.
7. Kill the heat and rest, covered, 10 minutes. Fluff, folding in the browned bits
   from the edges. Finish with scallions, parsley, and plenty of hot sauce at the
   table.

## Brown vs. red, and why it matters

The color of your jambalaya tells its whole story. If you want the deep,
savory-mahogany Cajun version, the work is in **step 2** — brown the meats
seriously and don't wipe the pot. If you want the brighter, tomato-kissed Creole
version, it's a friendlier, more forgiving cook. Neither is "authentic" at the
other's expense; Louisiana contains both.

## Make it yours

- **Add shrimp** in the last 5 minutes for a seafood version — stir them in on top
  so they steam gently.
- The classic party protein trio is chicken + sausage + shrimp.
- A spoonful of the fond-scraping deglaze with a splash of stock is the single
  biggest flavor upgrade — never leave that browned layer behind.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Jambalaya vs. gumbo
Not the same dish. In **jambalaya** the rice cooks *in* the pot and absorbs the
liquid. **Gumbo** is a thickened stew *served over* separately cooked rice. Don't
mix them up at a Louisiana table.
:::
